title: Sebastian and the Kitchen
premise: Felix Eastwick, a lighthouse keeper's grandson and part-time novelist, has spent ten years writing letters to a stranger named Sebastian — the only love he allows himself, safely fictional and safely past tense. When the real Sebastian buys the cottage next door, Felix discovers the letters were never anonymous: Sebastian has known who he was all along, and moved to Saltmere Bay to finally answer them in person. As the last ferry of the season approaches, Felix must decide whether the sentence he has rehearsed for a decade — 'I loved you before I ever met you' — can survive being spoken in the present tense. He says it on the dock as the ferry sounds its horn, and Sebastian stays.
about_author: E. M. Okonkwo is a former archivist who grew up in coastal towns and writes about the things people preserve instead of say. This is their third novel and first romance.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Distance
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Establishes his ritual: mornings at the lighthouse museum, evenings writing letters to 'Sebastian,' a character he insists is fiction. His editor wants a romance novel; Felix keeps killing every happy ending. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as discipline.

chapters.title: Sold, With Conditions
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. The neighboring cottage — empty since his grandfather's death — sells to an unknown buyer. The estate agent mentions the buyer asked specifically about the lighthouse and the ferry schedule. Felix feels watched by coincidence. Beat: unease beneath routine.

chapters.title: A Man With Familiar Hands
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. First sight of the new neighbor unloading boxes: dark coat, ink-stained fingers, a face that stops Felix mid-sentence. He looks exactly as Felix has imagined Sebastian for ten years. Beat: vertigo — the imaginary made flesh.

chapters.title: Sebastian
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Introduces himself with the name Felix gave his character; watches Felix realize it. He is warm, unhurried, and knows too much — the name of Felix's dog from childhood, the smell of his grandfather's pipe. Beat: charm laced with threat.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Postmarks
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, flashback chapter. How the letters began: grief after his sister's death, a wrong address, a reply from a stranger who kept writing back. We learn Felix never knew the correspondent's identity — until now. Beat: tenderness excavated from guilt.

chapters.title: The Cottage Next Door
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Sebastian invites Felix for tea; the cottage interior mirrors details from the letters — the blue door, the chipped teapot. Felix accuses him of theft or stalking. Sebastian only says, 'Read your own letters again.' Beat: suspicion hardening into fear.

chapters.title: What the Letters Never Said
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. He rereads a decade of correspondence and finds what he missed: replies that answered questions he never wrote down, knowledge of days no letter covered. Someone was near him the whole time. Beat: the past tense cracking.

chapters.title: Marguerite Knows Something
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. His grandmother Marguerite, keeper of family memory, goes quiet when Sebastian's name comes up. She warns Felix: 'Some people come back to collect.' Beat: generational dread; hint that survival in this family has always had a price.

chapters.title: The Ferry Timetable
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. We learn his side: he was the lighthouse keeper's apprentice decades ago, the boy Felix's sister loved, and the letters were his way back after exile. The last ferry of the season is in three weeks; after that, the bay is cut off till spring. Beat: stakes made concrete.

chapters.title: Drafts
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. He tries to write the confrontation into his novel and cannot. His editor rejects the manuscript: 'You keep saving everyone except yourself.' Felix burns nothing but sleeps badly. Beat: art failing where honesty is required.

chapters.title: Storm Glass
chapters.summary: Both POVs. A storm strands Felix and Sebastian together at the lighthouse. Forced proximity strips politeness; they argue about truth, debt, and who owes whom a decade. Almost-kiss interrupted by the storm lamp failing. Beat: desire and anger fused.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV (single departure). Reveals the family secret: the accident that killed Felix's sister involved Sebastian's father, and the Eastwicks took compensation money to stay silent — the inheritance Felix lives on. Beat: the ground giving way under everything.

chapters.title: Blood Money
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Confronts Marguerite, then Sebastian: was this all restitution? Sebastian admits he came to give the money back — and stayed because of the letters' author. Felix, unable to separate love from debt, walks out. Beat: midpoint collapse.

chapters.title: Wintering
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Two weeks of silence. He drafts the farewell letter he should have written years ago and cannot finish it. The village notices the estrangement; the ferry's last run is announced for Saturday. Beat: grief rehearsing itself.

chapters.title: The Unsent Pile
chapters.summary: Sebastian, POV. Packing to leave, Sebastian shows us his own unsent letters — forty-one drafts answering Felix over the years, each one stopped by shame about his father. He decides Felix deserves the whole archive, not a curated version. Beat: humility as courage.

chapters.title: Everything I Never Posted
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Sebastian leaves the box of drafts on Felix's doorstep without a note. Felix reads through the night, watching his own decade reflected back — including the draft dated the week his sister died, soaked with rain. Beat: catharsis through evidence.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Friday. Felix rehearses the sentence aloud to the empty lighthouse, to Marguerite, to the sea. Marguerite gives him her blessing and her confession both: 'We bought our safety with your silence. Don't buy yours the same way.' Beat: resolve assembled from wreckage.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Saturday morning. Sebastian waits at the dock with a ticket; Felix runs the cliff path as the horn sounds. The crowd, the gulls, the engine noise — everything conspires against speech. Beat: rising action cresting.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. On the gangway, Felix says it: 'I loved you before I ever met you — and I'm saying it now, in the present tense.' Sebastian steps off the ferry onto the dock, letting it leave without him. Beat: climax; the sentence lands.

chapters.title: What Stays When the Boats Stop
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The bay settles into its winter isolation. First awkward, ordinary days of actually knowing each other — dishes, silences, arguments about whose letters were worse. Beat: intimacy without distance for the first time.

chapters.title: The Last Chapter He Wrote Alone
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Felix finishes the novel at last, changing the ending so the lovers meet in time. He mails it to his editor with a note: 'This one's nonfiction now.' Marguerite and Sebastian share tea; old debts are spoken of plainly. Beat: reconciliation across generations.

chapters.title: Spring Tide
chapters.summary: Both POVs, epilogue. The first ferry of the new season arrives carrying Felix's published book. On the dock, Sebastian reads the dedication — 'For S., who answered' — and Felix watches him understand it. Final line echoes the opening letter. Beat: quiet joy; memory transformed from burden to inheritance worth keeping.
